Far-field results require this boundary; without it there is no surface to integrate and the antenna reports nothing.

tools.name: hfss.wave_port / hfss.lumped_port
tools.description: Create excitations from PyAEDT. Both take an existing sheet, or a pair of objects from which PyAEDT builds the port sheet itself between their closest faces, and both return a port object whose name becomes the S-parameter index. wave_port solves a 2D modal problem on the sheet and is correct for coax, waveguide and any port on the model boundary; lumped_port imposes a uniform field across an internal gap and is the pragmatic choice for feeds inside the model.
tools.usage:
port = hfss.wave_port(assignment, reference=None, create_port_sheet=False,
                     integration_line=None, impedance=50, num_modes=1,
                     name=None, renormalize=True, deembed=0)
port = hfss.lumped_port(assignment, reference=None, create_port_sheet=False,
                        integration_line=None, impedance=50, name=None, renormalize=True)

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: The port sheet by name or handle, a face ID, or - with create_port_sheet True - the signal conductor whose face the sheet is built on.

parameters.name: reference
parameters.description: The return conductor, used when PyAEDT creates the sheet itself and to define terminals in a Terminal solution type.

parameters.name: create_port_sheet
parameters.description: True lets PyAEDT construct the sheet between the two named objects instead of requiring one to exist.

parameters.name: integration_line
parameters.description: Direction of the impedance line, given as hfss.AxisDir.XPos / ZNeg and similar, or as an explicit pair of points. It fixes the mode's sign and its Zpi impedance.

parameters.name: impedance
parameters.description: Reference impedance in ohms for renormalisation, normally 50.

parameters.name: num_modes
parameters.description: Modes solved by a wave port. One for coax and microstrip; overmoded waveguide and multi-conductor lines need more.

parameters.name: deembed
parameters.description: Distance the reference plane is shifted along the port normal, removing a length of uniform feed line from the S-parameters.

tools.example:
# Wave port on the end face of the coax
port1 = hfss.wave_port(assignment="PortSheet",
                       integration_line=hfss.AxisDir.XPos,
                       impedance=50, num_modes=1, name="P1")

# Lumped port built automatically between trace and ground
port2 = hfss.lumped_port(assignment="Trace", reference="Gnd",
                         create_port_sheet=True,
                         integration_line=hfss.AxisDir.ZNeg,
                         impedance=50, name="P2")

print(hfss.excitation_names)
print(port1.name, port1.props["NumModes"])
tools.notes: Without an integration line a wave port still solves, but its Zpi impedance and the sign of the mode are arbitrary, which shows up as an S-parameter that is right in magnitude and wrong in phase. Older PyAEDT exposed create_wave_port_between_objects and create_lumped_port_between_objects; the shorter names arrived with the ansys.aedt.core rename. In Terminal solution types the reference conductor determines the terminal names used in every report.

tools.name: hfss.mesh.assign_length_mesh / hfss.mesh.assign_skin_depth
tools.description: Seed the initial mesh where the adaptive refinement would otherwise start too coarse. assign_length_mesh caps element size, and optionally element count, on named objects or faces - the tool for thin gaps, small features and curved surfaces. assign_skin_depth builds graded layers into a conductor so that current crowding into the skin depth is resolved, which matters whenever loss, not just matching, is the answer being computed.
tools.usage:
op = hfss.mesh.assign_length_mesh(assignment, inside_selection=True,
                                  maximum_length=1, maximum_elements=1000, name=None)
op = hfss.mesh.assign_skin_depth(assignment, skin_depth, maximum_elements=None,
                                 layers_number="2", name=None)

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: Object names, handles or face IDs the operation applies to.

parameters.name: inside_selection
parameters.description: True refines the volume inside the selection; False refines only its surface, which is usually enough and far cheaper.

parameters.name: maximum_length
parameters.description: Largest allowed element edge, as a number in model units or a unit string. Set it from the feature size, not from the wavelength.

parameters.name: maximum_elements
parameters.description: Hard cap on elements generated by this operation, so a mistaken length does not explode the mesh.

parameters.name: skin_depth
parameters.description: The skin depth at the frequency of interest, e.g. "1.3um" for copper at 2.45 GHz. Layers are graded from it.

parameters.name: layers_number
parameters.description: How many layers are stacked into the conductor; two or three is normal, more only for tightly coupled lossy structures.

parameters.name: hfss.mesh.meshoperations
parameters.description: List of the operations defined, each with .name, .props and delete(), so a script can audit or replace them.

tools.example:
hfss.mesh.assign_length_mesh(["FeedGap"],
                             inside_selection=True,
                             maximum_length="0.2mm",
                             maximum_elements=20000,
                             name="GapSeed")

hfss.mesh.assign_skin_depth(["Trace"],
                            skin_depth="1.3um",
                            layers_number="3",
                            name="TraceSkin")

for op in hfss.mesh.meshoperations:
    print(op.name, op.type)
tools.notes: Mesh operations only seed the initial mesh; adaptive refinement then drives convergence, so over-seeding wastes memory without improving the answer. A skin-depth operation is pointless on a body whose solve_inside is False, because there is no interior mesh to grade. assign_initial_mesh_from_slider sets the global initial-mesh quality when a whole model needs to start finer.

tools.name: hfss.create_setup / create_linear_count_sweep / create_linear_step_sweep / create_single_point_sweep
tools.description: Define the solution from PyAEDT. create_setup returns a Setup object whose props dictionary mirrors the native InsertSetup array exactly, so anything available in the dialog can be set and pushed back with update(). The three sweep helpers then add a frequency sweep to that setup by count, by step size, or at a single frequency, wrapping the RangeType/RangeStart/RangeEnd bookkeeping of the object model.
tools.usage:
setup = hfss.create_setup(name="Setup1")
setup.props["Frequency"] = "2.45GHz"
setup.update()
hfss.create_linear_count_sweep(setup, units, start_frequency, stop_frequency,
                               num_of_freq_points, name=None, sweep_type="Interpolating")
hfss.create_linear_step_sweep(setup, unit, start_frequency, stop_frequency, step_size, ...)
hfss.create_single_point_sweep(setup, unit, freq, save_fields=True, ...)

parameters.name: setup.props
parameters.description: Dictionary of the native setup properties: "Frequency", "MaxDeltaS", "MaximumPasses", "MinimumConvergedPasses", "BasisOrder". Call update() to push changes to AEDT.

parameters.name: start_frequency / stop_frequency
parameters.description: Band limits as plain numbers interpreted in the units argument, e.g. 2 and 3 with units="GHz".

parameters.name: num_of_freq_points / step_size
parameters.description: Sweep resolution: a point count for the linear-count form, or an increment such as 0.01 for the linear-step form.

parameters.name: sweep_type
parameters.description: "Interpolating" fits a rational model from a few solved points and is the default choice; "Discrete" solves every point; "Fast" builds a single-point reduced-order model.

parameters.name: save_fields / save_rad_fields
parameters.description: Whether field data is retained at swept frequencies. Leaving these on across a wide sweep is the usual cause of a results folder in the hundreds of gigabytes.

parameters.name: create_single_point_sweep
parameters.description: Solves one frequency and, with save_single_field True, keeps its fields - the cheap way to get a field plot at a design frequency without a full sweep.

tools.example:
setup = hfss.create_setup(name="Setup1")
setup.props["Frequency"] = "2.45GHz"
setup.props["MaximumPasses"] = 12
setup.props["MaxDeltaS"] = 0.02
setup.update()

hfss.create_linear_count_sweep(setup="Setup1", units="GHz",
                               start_frequency=2, stop_frequency=3,
                               num_of_freq_points=401,
                               name="Sweep1", sweep_type="Interpolating",
                               save_fields=False)

hfss.create_single_point_sweep(setup="Setup1", unit="GHz", freq=2.45,
                               name="AtResonance", save_single_field=True)

print([s.name for s in hfss.setups])
tools.notes: Keyword names moved with the ansys.aedt.core rename: older scripts pass setupname, unit, freqstart and freqstop. Reports address the results as "Setup1 : Sweep1", or "Setup1 : LastAdaptive" for the converged adaptive solution, and getting that string wrong is the usual reason a report is empty. An interpolating sweep that will not converge almost always means the adaptive solution at the mesh frequency is not converged either.

tools.name: hfss.analyze / hfss.analyze_setup
tools.description: Run the solver. analyze() with no arguments solves every setup in the design, while analyze_setup(name) solves one - which is also how a named Optimetrics study is launched. Both accept the HPC arguments that would otherwise come from the Analysis Options dialog, so a script can ask for a specific number of cores, parallel tasks and GPUs without touching the saved preferences.
tools.usage:
hfss.analyze(setup=None, cores=4, tasks=1, gpus=0, use_auto_settings=True)
hfss.analyze_setup(name, cores=4, tasks=1, gpus=0)

parameters.name: setup / name
parameters.description: Setup or sweep to solve. Omitting it in analyze() solves everything in the design, including parametric studies.

parameters.name: cores
parameters.description: Cores given to the solver. Beyond the base licence this consumes HPC tasks, so the number has to match what the licence pool allows.

parameters.name: tasks
parameters.description: Parallel tasks for distributed solving - frequency points, domains or parametric variations solved side by side. Needs a distributed HPC licence to be worth more than 1.

parameters.name: gpus
parameters.description: GPUs to use where the solver supports acceleration, notably the transient and SBR+ solvers.

parameters.name: use_auto_settings
parameters.description: Let AEDT choose how to spread cores over tasks and domains rather than pinning the split by hand.

parameters.name: hfss.save_project()
parameters.description: Call before analyzing: the solver writes its mesh and field data into the results folder next to the saved .aedt file.

tools.example:
hfss.save_project()

hfss.analyze_setup("Setup1", cores=8, tasks=1)

# Everything, including sweeps and Optimetrics studies
hfss.analyze(cores=8, tasks=2, use_auto_settings=True)

# Convergence data for the run that just finished
setup = hfss.get_setup("Setup1")
print(setup.is_solved)
tools.notes: The call blocks for the whole solve, so a PyAEDT script that solves a large model ties up the interpreter for hours; for production runs build and post-process with PyAEDT but hand the solve to ansysedt -ng -BatchSolve under a scheduler. Older releases named the arguments num_cores, num_tasks and num_gpu. Asking for more cores than the HPC licence allows makes the solve fail at start-up rather than fall back.

tools.name: hfss.post.create_report / hfss.post.get_solution_data / hfss.post.export_report_to_csv
tools.description: The post-processing trio. create_report builds a plot in the design tree from an expression list; get_solution_data returns the same numbers as a SolutionData object without creating any plot, which is what a script that computes bandwidth or finds a resonance actually wants; export_report_to_csv writes an existing report's traces to disk. All three understand the report categories, so the same idiom covers S-parameters, far fields and antenna parameters.
tools.usage:
rep = hfss.post.create_report(expressions, setup_sweep_name=None, domain="Sweep",
                              primary_sweep_variable=None, report_category=None,
                              plot_type="Rectangular Plot", context=None, plot_name=None)
data = hfss.post.get_solution_data(expressions, setup_sweep_name=None, domain="Sweep",
                                   variations=None, report_category=None, context=None)
hfss.post.export_report_to_csv(project_dir, plot_name)

parameters.name: expressions
parameters.description: Trace expressions such as "dB(S(P1,P1))", "re(Z(P1,P1))", "GainTotal" - the port names come from the excitations.

parameters.name: setup_sweep_name
parameters.description: "Setup1 : Sweep1" for swept data or "Setup1 : LastAdaptive" for the converged adaptive solution. Defaults to the design's nominal sweep.

parameters.name: report_category
parameters.description: "Modal Solution Data", "Terminal Solution Data", "Far Fields", "Antenna Parameters" or "Fields", matching the design's solution type.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Extra scope for the report - the name of an infinite sphere for a far-field plot, or a polyline for a field-along-line plot.

parameters.name: variations
parameters.description: Dictionary pinning design variables and sweep values, e.g. {"patch_l": "Nominal", "Freq": ["All"]}, used to slice a parametric solution.

parameters.name: SolutionData object
parameters.description: Exposes primary_sweep_values, data_real(), data_magnitude(), data_db20() and export_data_to_csv() - plain Python lists for further analysis.

parameters.name: plot_type
parameters.description: "Rectangular Plot", "Smith Chart", "Polar Plot", "3D Polar Plot" or "Data Table".

tools.example:
hfss.post.create_report("dB(S(P1,P1))", plot_name="S11")

data = hfss.post.get_solution_data(expressions="dB(S(P1,P1))",
                                   setup_sweep_name="Setup1 : Sweep1")
freqs = data.primary_sweep_values
s11 = data.data_db20()

f_res = freqs[s11.index(min(s11))]
band = [f for f, v in zip(freqs, s11) if v <= -10]
print(f"resonance {f_res} GHz, -10 dB band {band[0]} to {band[-1]} GHz")

hfss.post.export_report_to_csv(r"C:/work/reports", "S11")
tools.notes: get_solution_data is the right tool inside an automation loop: it needs no plot, works in non-graphical mode and returns ordinary lists. Far-field expressions need report_category="Far Fields" and the context set to an infinite sphere name, otherwise the request is rejected rather than returning empty. data.export_data_to_csv writes the same numbers without going through a report object.

tools.name: hfss.post.create_fieldplot_surface / hfss.post.create_fieldplot_volume
tools.description: Create field overlays on geometry - surface current on a patch, |E| through a substrate, near field in an air region - and get back a plot object that can be styled, exported as an image or rendered offscreen. The quantity is any field name or a named expression built in the Fields Calculator, and the intrinsics pin the frequency and phase at which the field is evaluated. These plots are the visual counterpart to the numbers get_solution_data returns.
tools.usage:
plot = hfss.post.create_fieldplot_surface(assignment, quantity, setup=None,
                                          intrinsics=None, name=None)
plot = hfss.post.create_fieldplot_volume(assignment, quantity, setup=None,
                                         intrinsics=None, name=None)

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: Object or sheet names, or face IDs, the plot is drawn on. The volume form takes solids and fills their interior.

parameters.name: quantity
parameters.description: Field quantity: "Mag_E", "Mag_H", "Mag_Jsurf", "ComplexMag_E", or a named expression previously defined in the Fields Calculator.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Solution the field comes from, normally "Setup1 : LastAdaptive". A sweep frequency only works if that sweep saved fields.

parameters.name: intrinsics
parameters.description: Dictionary pinning the evaluation point, e.g. {"Freq": "2.45GHz", "Phase": "0deg"}. Sweeping phase is how an animation is built.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Plot name in the Field Overlays tree, used later to update, export or delete it.

parameters.name: plot.export_image(...)
parameters.description: Writes a picture of the plot; hfss.post.plot_field renders offscreen with PyVista, which works in non-graphical runs.

tools.example:
hfss.post.create_fieldplot_surface(
    assignment=["Patch"],
    quantity="Mag_Jsurf",
    setup="Setup1 : LastAdaptive",
    intrinsics={"Freq": "2.45GHz", "Phase": "0deg"},
    name="PatchCurrent")

vol = hfss.post.create_fieldplot_volume(
    assignment=["Sub"],
    quantity="Mag_E",
    setup="Setup1 : LastAdaptive",
    intrinsics={"Freq": "2.45GHz", "Phase": "0deg"},
    name="SubstrateE")

vol.export_image(r"C:/work/reports/substrate_e.png")
tools.notes: A plot that comes back empty almost always means the solution has no stored fields at that frequency: the adaptive pass always keeps them, a sweep only does when save_fields was True. Older releases spelled the arguments objlist, quantityName, setup_name and intrinsincDict, and rendered with plot_field_from_fieldplot. Named expressions from the Fields Calculator can be used as the quantity, which is how derived plots such as normalised |E| are made.

tools.name: hfss.insert_infinite_sphere / hfss.export_touchstone
tools.description: The two result-generating calls that close an antenna or network run. insert_infinite_sphere defines the far-field sphere over which patterns, gain, directivity and antenna parameters are computed - without one, no far-field report can be created. export_touchstone writes the solved S-parameter matrix to a .sNp file, which is how the result leaves HFSS for a circuit simulator, a correlation script or a datasheet.
tools.usage:
sphere = hfss.insert_infinite_sphere(definition="Theta-Phi",
                                    x_start=0, x_stop=180, x_step=10,
                                    y_start=-180, y_stop=180, y_step=10,
                                    units="deg", name="3D")
hfss.export_touchstone(setup=None, sweep=None, output_file=None, variations=None)

parameters.name: definition
parameters.description: Angular parameterisation of the sphere, normally "Theta-Phi". The x_ arguments then sweep theta and the y_ arguments phi.

parameters.name: x_start / x_stop / x_step
parameters.description: Theta range and resolution in degrees. 0 to 180 in 10 degree steps is a reasonable 3D pattern; 1 degree steps for a principal-plane cut.

parameters.name: y_start / y_stop / y_step
parameters.description: Phi range and resolution. Restricting phi to 0 and 90 gives just the two principal planes at a fraction of the cost.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Sphere name, which is what a far-field report passes as its context.

parameters.name: setup / sweep
parameters.description: Which solution to export from, e.g. "Setup1" and "Sweep1". Omitted, the nominal setup and its sweep are used.

parameters.name: output_file
parameters.description: Destination path. The extension follows the port count - .s1p, .s2p, .s4p - and AEDT corrects it if it does not match.

parameters.name: variations
parameters.description: Which parametric variations to export; a swept design otherwise exports only the nominal one.

tools.example:
hfss.insert_infinite_sphere(definition="Theta-Phi",
                            x_start=0, x_stop=180, x_step=2,
                            y_start=-180, y_stop=180, y_step=2,
                            units="deg", name="3D")

pattern = hfss.post.get_solution_data(expressions="GainTotal",
                                      setup_sweep_name="Setup1 : LastAdaptive",
                                      report_category="Far Fields",
                                      context="3D",
                                      variations={"Freq": ["2.45GHz"], "Phi": ["0deg"]})
print(max(pattern.data_db20()))

hfss.export_touchstone(setup="Setup1", sweep="Sweep1",
                       output_file=r"C:/work/patch.s1p")
tools.notes: A far-field sphere is only meaningful when a radiation, PML or FE-BI boundary exists; on a closed model the report returns nothing. Fine angular steps multiply post-processing time and file size, so use a coarse 3D sphere plus separate fine cuts. The native equivalents are oModule("RadField").InsertInfiniteSphereSetup and oModule("Solutions").ExportNetworkData, the latter taking positional rather than name/value arguments.

tools.name: hfss.parametrics.add / hfss.optimizations.add
tools.description: Wrap the solver in a study. parametrics.add creates an Optimetrics parametric sweep over a design variable, to which output calculations are attached with add_calculation; optimizations.add creates an optimisation, sensitivity or statistical study driven by a cost function built from a report expression. Both return setup objects whose props can be edited, and both are then solved like any other setup by name.
tools.usage:
param = hfss.parametrics.add(variable, start_point, end_point=None, step=None,
                             variation_type="LinearStep")
param.add_calculation(calculation="dB(S(1,1))", ranges={"Freq": "2.45GHz"})
opt = hfss.optimizations.add(calculation, ranges=None, optimization_type="Optimization")
hfss.analyze_setup(param.name)

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: Design variable to sweep. It must already exist, which is why the geometry has to be built parametrically from the start.

parameters.name: start_point / end_point / step
parameters.description: Sweep definition as expression strings with units, e.g. "27mm", "31mm", "0.5mm".

parameters.name: variation_type
parameters.description: "LinearStep", "LinearCount", "LogScale" or "SingleValue" - the same range forms as a frequency sweep.

parameters.name: add_calculation(calculation, ranges)
parameters.description: Attaches an output expression evaluated at the given sweep point, e.g. dB(S(1,1)) at 2.45 GHz, so the study table carries a result per variation.

parameters.name: calculation / ranges
parameters.description: For an optimisation, the cost expression and where it is evaluated. Goals and conditions then live in opt.props["Goals"].

parameters.name: optimization_type
parameters.description: "Optimization", "Sensitivity" or "Statistical". Optimisers available include Quasi Newton, Pattern Search, Sequential Non-linear Programming and Genetic Algorithm.

parameters.name: hfss.parametrics / hfss.optimizations
parameters.description: Collections of the studies defined in the design, each entry carrying .name, .props and delete().

tools.example:
hfss["patch_l"] = "29mm"

param = hfss.parametrics.add("patch_l",
                             start_point="27mm", end_point="31mm",
                             step="0.5mm", variation_type="LinearStep")
param.add_calculation(calculation="dB(S(P1,P1))", ranges={"Freq": "2.45GHz"})
hfss.analyze_setup(param.name)

data = hfss.post.get_solution_data(expressions="dB(S(P1,P1))",
                                   setup_sweep_name="Setup1 : Sweep1",
                                   variations={"patch_l": ["All"], "Freq": ["2.45GHz"]})

opt = hfss.optimizations.add(calculation="dB(S(P1,P1))",
                             ranges={"Freq": "2.45GHz"},
                             optimization_type="Optimization")
tools.notes: A parametric sweep solves the full model once per variation, so the results folder grows linearly with the point count - disable field saving unless a variation's fields are genuinely needed. Optimisation on an electromagnetic cost function is expensive; a coarse parametric sweep first, then a local optimisation from the best point, converges far faster than optimising from a guess. Larger design-space studies are usually better driven from optiSLang or Workbench DesignXplorer.

tools.name: ansysedt -RunScriptAndExit / -RunScript
tools.description: Run a scripting file from the command line. -RunScriptAndExit executes the script and closes the desktop afterwards, which is the standard headless entry point for model generation, batch post-processing and regression runs; -RunScript executes it and leaves the session open so the result can be inspected. Combined with -ng the whole thing runs without a graphical interface, which is what a build server or a scheduler needs.
tools.usage:
ansysedt [-ng] -RunScriptAndExit <script.py|script.vbs>
ansysedt -RunScript <script.py>

parameters.name: -RunScriptAndExit
parameters.description: Execute the script and quit, returning the licence. The right choice for unattended runs.

parameters.name: -RunScript
parameters.description: Execute the script and keep the session open, for debugging a script against a visible model.

parameters.name: -ng
parameters.description: No graphics. Faster and required on headless servers; the script must then avoid anything that opens a dialog.

parameters.name: <script>
parameters.description: A .py file run by the embedded IronPython engine or a .vbs file run by the VBScript engine. It must begin with ScriptEnv.Initialize to bind oDesktop.

parameters.name: -features=beta
parameters.description: Enable beta features for the session, needed when a recorded script touches options that are still pre-release.

parameters.name: -waitforlicense
parameters.description: Queue instead of failing when no licence is free, which keeps a scheduler job from dying on a busy pool.

tools.example:
# Windows
"C:\Program Files\AnsysEM\v251\Win64\ansysedt.exe" -ng -RunScriptAndExit C:\work\build_antenna.py

# Linux: always go through the wrapper script, not the raw executable
/opt/ansys_inc/v251/AnsysEM/ansysedt -ng -RunScriptAndExit /work/build_antenna.py

# Keep the session open to inspect the result
ansysedt -RunScript C:\work\build_antenna.py
tools.notes: This route runs the script in AEDT's own embedded interpreter, so it sees oDesktop directly but is limited to the bundled IronPython and cannot import arbitrary CPython packages. A PyAEDT script is the opposite: run it as an ordinary CPython program, and it starts or attaches to AEDT itself, which is why numpy, pandas and matplotlib are available there. On Linux the ansysedt wrapper in v251/AnsysEM sets up the environment; calling the binary directly usually fails.

tools.name: ansysedt -ScriptArgs
tools.description: Pass arguments into a script run from the command line, so one script can serve many parameter sets instead of being edited per run. The whole argument list is given as a single quoted string, which the script splits itself, and it is read inside the script from the ScriptArgument property that AEDT sets up alongside oDesktop. This is what makes a recorded script usable from a scheduler loop.
tools.usage: ansysedt [-ng] -RunScriptAndExit <script.py> -ScriptArgs "<arg1,arg2,...>"

parameters.name: -ScriptArgs "..."
parameters.description: One quoted string handed to the script. Pack several values in with a delimiter of your choice, since only one argument string is passed.

parameters.name: ScriptArgument
parameters.description: The name under which the string is available inside an IronPython script once ScriptEnv.Initialize has run.

parameters.name: Quoting
parameters.description: Quote the whole string at the shell level; on Windows avoid unescaped double quotes inside it, and prefer commas or semicolons as separators.

parameters.name: sys.argv
parameters.description: The CPython alternative: a PyAEDT script launched as an ordinary Python program takes its arguments through argparse or sys.argv instead.

tools.example:
# Launch:
#   ansysedt -ng -RunScriptAndExit C:\work\sweep.py -ScriptArgs "2.45GHz,50,Setup1"

import ScriptEnv
ScriptEnv.Initialize("Ansoft.ElectronicsDesktop")

freq, imped, setup = ScriptArgument.split(",")
oDesktop.AddMessage("", "", 0, "building at " + freq + " into " + imped + " ohm")

oProject = oDesktop.NewProject()
oProject.InsertDesign("HFSS", "Auto", "DrivenModal", "")
oDesign = oProject.SetActiveDesign("Auto")
oDesign.ChangeProperty(
    ["NAME:AllTabs",
     ["NAME:LocalVariableTab",
      ["NAME:PropServers", "LocalVariables"],
      ["NAME:NewProps",
       ["NAME:f0", "PropType:=", "VariableProp", "UserDef:=", True, "Value:=", freq]]]])
oProject.SaveAs("C:/work/auto_" + freq + ".aedt", True)
tools.notes: Only one -ScriptArgs string is delivered, so anything structured has to be encoded into it - a comma-separated list, or a path to a JSON file the script then reads. For a PyAEDT workflow this switch is unnecessary: run the script with python and use argparse, which is easier to test outside AEDT entirely.

tools.name: ansysedt -ng -BatchSolve
tools.description: Solve a project headless from the command line, which is how production runs and scheduler jobs are done. With no qualifier it solves every design and setup in the project; a Design:Variation:Setup qualifier restricts it to one. -batchoptions overrides registry-backed solve options such as core counts and distributed behaviour for that run only, and -Distributed with -machinelist spreads the job across machines.
tools.usage:
ansysedt -ng [-monitor] -BatchSolve ["<Design>:<Variation>:<Setup>"] <project.aedt>
ansysedt -ng -BatchSolve -Distributed -machinelist list="host1:4,host2:4" -auto <project.aedt>
ansysedt -ng -BatchSolve -batchoptions "'HFSS/NumCoresPerDistributedTask'=4" <project.aedt>

parameters.name: -BatchSolve
parameters.description: Solve and exit. Without a qualifier every design and setup in the project is solved, including Optimetrics studies.

parameters.name: "<Design>:<Variation>:<Setup>"
parameters.description: Restrict the solve, e.g. "HFSSDesign1:Nominal:Setup1". Use it in queue scripts so each scheduler job owns exactly one setup.

parameters.name: -batchoptions
parameters.description: Quoted 'path/Key'=value pairs overriding solve options for this run, or the name of an options file. Nothing in the saved preferences is changed.

parameters.name: -Distributed / -machinelist
parameters.description: Spread the solve over several machines, listed as host:cores pairs or as a total task count; -auto lets AEDT pick the distribution strategy.

parameters.name: -monitor
parameters.description: Write solver progress to the console so a scheduler log shows adaptive passes and sweep points instead of going silent.

parameters.name: -waitforlicense
parameters.description: Wait for a licence rather than failing immediately, which keeps queued jobs alive on a contended pool.

tools.example:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hfss_patch
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8

ANSYSEM=/opt/ansys_inc/v251/AnsysEM

$ANSYSEM/ansysedt -ng -monitor -waitforlicense \
  -distributed -machinelist num=$SLURM_NTASKS -auto \
  -batchoptions "'HFSS/NumCoresPerDistributedTask'=8" \
  -BatchSolve "HFSSDesign1:Nominal:Setup1" $PWD/patch.aedt

# Post-process afterwards with a PyAEDT script that only reads results
python extract_s11.py $PWD/patch.aedt
tools.notes: The usual production split is: build the model with PyAEDT, solve with -ng -BatchSolve under the scheduler, then post-process with a second PyAEDT script that opens the solved project read-only. Solving through an interactive PyAEDT analyze() call instead ties the licence and the interpreter to the job for its whole duration. Option keys passed to -batchoptions are the registry paths shown in the HPC and Analysis Options dialog, so record the settings in the GUI first.

tools.name: Tools > Record Script To File / Tools > Run Script
tools.description: The discovery mechanism for the entire object model, and the reason AEDT scripting is practical at all. Record Script To File starts capturing; every GUI action afterwards is written out as the exact scripting call with its full argument array, including the property names a dialog sets behind the scenes. Run Script replays a .py or .vbs file. Because the argument arrays are long, deeply nested and version-sensitive, recording an action and then parameterising the recording is far more reliable than writing calls from memory.
tools.usage:
Tools > Record Script To File...   (choose a .py or .vbs destination)
<perform the action in the GUI>
Tools > Stop Script Recording
Tools > Run Script...              (or the Scripts ribbon / Automation tab)

parameters.name: Record Script To File
parameters.description: Starts recording to a chosen file. Everything from a dialog OK to a mouse-driven geometry edit is captured as a scripting call.

parameters.name: Stop Script Recording
parameters.description: Ends the capture and closes the file. Recording adds overhead, so stop it before doing anything large.

parameters.name: Run Script
parameters.description: Executes a script file in the embedded interpreter against the current session, the GUI equivalent of -RunScript.

parameters.name: Script language
parameters.description: Whether recording produces Python or VBScript is set in Tools > Options > General Options; Python is the sensible default for new work.

parameters.name: Scripts / Automation ribbon
parameters.description: Where saved scripts, PyAEDT toolkits and custom menu entries are launched from once a script is worth keeping.

tools.example:
# Workflow
# 1. Tools > Record Script To File...  ->  assign_port.py
# 2. Assign a wave port with an integration line in the GUI
# 3. Tools > Stop Script Recording
# 4. Edit the recording: replace literals with variables, wrap it in a function
# 5. Tools > Run Script, or call the same array from PyAEDT

# The recorded call, parameterised and replayed through PyAEDT:
oModule = hfss.odesign.GetModule("BoundarySetup")
oModule.AssignWavePort(
    ["NAME:" + port_name,
     "Objects:=", [sheet_name],
     "NumModes:=", 1,
     "RenormalizeAllTerminals:=", True,
     "DoDeembed:=", False,
     ["NAME:Modes",
      ["NAME:Mode1", "ModeNum:=", 1, "UseIntLine:=", True,
       ["NAME:IntLine", "Start:=", line_start, "End:=", line_end],
       "CharImp:=", "Zpi"]]])
tools.notes: Recording captures only what the GUI actually does, so an action that produces no call - selecting an object, changing the view - records nothing, and a recorded script always refers to objects by the names they had at record time. It is the only dependable source for the argument arrays of dialogs PyAEDT does not yet wrap, and the recommended first step whenever a call raises an unhelpful COM error.
